Analysis of Substance Abuse and Opioid Use Among Screened Inmates in Pennsylvania by Year and Gender

Ainsley Carlson

2025-09-30

1 Introduction

In this report two types of analysis will be completed. The first, will explore if the percent of admissions with a diagnosed substance abuse problem is related to the percent of admissions with opioid usage controlling for year. Additionally, I will observe if the effects of gender, county, average Texas Christian University (TCU) drug score, and number of drug screened admissions have a significant effect on the relationship between percent of admissions with a diagnosed substance abuse problem and percent of admissions with opioid use. This analysis will be done by create multiple linear regressions to determine the model with best fit and prediction abiltiy. The second analysis will use a logistic relationship to determine if there is a relationship between there being a high percentage of inmates tested with a substance abuse problem and the gender of the inmates. The variables mentioned above will also be tested to see if they are significant and add predictive value to the model. Additionally, I will also test if there is an interaction between opioid use and year for the logistic regression.

2 Dataset Information

This dataset comes from the Pennsylvania Department of Corrections and consists of quartley data from 2016 to the current year by county. Dataset includes inmate admissions, average Texas Christian University Drug Screen II (TCU) score, number and percent of inmate admissions who identify opioids as top three drug of choice, inmates with a substance abuse problem, and number and percent who used opioids in the year prior to admission. There 7,722 observations and 20 variables within the dataset.

2.1 Variable Descriptions

Geographic Area [Character]: Name of State or County delineating the data that is shown in this row.

County Name [Character]: County name from which the inmate was sentenced to the Pennsylvania Department of Corrections.

Gender [Character]: This is All for both male and female or just male or female delineating the data in the row.

Age [Character]: The age group for the data in the row.

Year and Quarter [Character]: The Year and Quarter of the data in the row.

Time Period Dates [Character]: The beginning and end date of the data in the row.

Calendar Year of Data [Numeric]: year

Drug Screened Admissions [Numeric]: Total number of new commit admissions with valid Texas Christian University Drug Screen II (TCU) scores

Average TCU Drug Screen Score [Numeric]: Average score on the Texas Christian University Drug Screens (TCU) among Department of Corrections (DOC) admissions who have scores. The TCU assesses for substance abuse issues and provides a score between 0 and 9. A score of 3 or higher indicates a substance use disorder. Link: http://ibr.tcu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/TCU-Drug-Screen-II-sg-v11.pdf

New Admissions with Opioid Use [Numeric]: Number of new court admissions who used opiates as their top three drugs of choice, based on the TCU assessment results. The TCU Drug Screen II is scored to produce a single total score which can range from 0 to 9. Score values of 3 or greater indicate relatively severe drug-related problems, and correspond approximately to DSM drug dependence diagnosis. Responses to Item 10 indicate which drug (or drugs) the respondent feels is primarily responsible for his or her drug-related problems.

Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use [Numeric]: Percent of total new court admissions who used opiates as their top three drugs of choice.

Admissions with Diagnosed Substance Abuse Problem [Numeric]: Number of new court admissions who had a TCU score of 3 or higher, indicating a substance abuse problem.The TCU Drug Screen II is scored to produce a single total score which can range from 0 to 9. Score values of 3 or greater indicate relatively severe drug-related problems, and correspond approximately to DSM drug dependence diagnosis. Responses to Item 10 indicate which drug (or drugs) the respondent feels is primarily responsible for his or her drug-related problems.

Percent of Admissions with Diagnosed Substance Abuse Problem [Numeric]: Percent of new court admissions who had a TCU score of 3 or higher, indicating a substance abuse problem. The TCU Drug Screen II is scored to produce a single total score which can range from 0 to 9. Score values of 3 or greater indicate relatively severe drug-related problems, and correspond approximately to DSM drug dependence diagnosis. Responses to Item 10 indicate which drug (or drugs) the respondent feels is primarily responsible for his or her drug-related problems.

Admissions with Opioid use in past 12 months [Numeric]: Number of new court admissions who self identified as using Opiates or Heroin in the prior 12 months before admission to DOC.

Percent of Admissions with Opioid use in past 12 months [Numeric]: Percent of total new court admissions who self identified as using Opiates or Heroin in the prior 12 months before admission to DOC

State FIPS [Numeric]: These are the first 2 digits of the 5-digit Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) code that designate the State association.

County FIPS [Numeric]: The 3-digit part of the 5-digit county FIPS code specifically standing for the county.

Latitude [Character]: A generic Latitude point within the county. A point is also provided for outside of the state (on a map it will sit to the southeast of the state). This number represents the total number for the state and this location provides a spot on a map to display the PA number without having it duplicate within a county when using in a mapping visual.

Longitude [Character]: A generic Longitude point within the county. A point is also provided for outside of the state (on a map it will sit to the southeast of the state). This number represents the total number for the state and this location provides a spot on a map to display the PA number without having it duplicate within a county when using in a mapping visual.

Georeferenced Latitude &Longitude [Character]:A generic georeferenced Latitude & Longitude point within the county. These points can be used to create visualizations such as maps to show the data by county. A point is also provided for outside of the state (on a map it will sit to the southeast of the state). This number represents the total number for the state and this location provides a spot on a map to display the PA number without having it duplicate within a county when using in a mapping visual.

3 Missing Values

None of the variables have missing values except for “Georeferenced Lattitude &Longitude”, which is not a variable of interest in out analysis. Therefore, there is no concern about what should be done with missing values and can proceed with the analysis.

3.1 Exploratory Data Analysis

3.1.1 Gender

Looking at the number of new inmates who recieved a drug screening shows there is about 8 times as men as women, which is why it is important to use the percentages when looking at the amount who used opioid and/or had a substance abuse problem. Additionally, having a larger sample of men could lead to unequal comparisons between the genders, specifically on the county level. Looking at the overall state level there should not be and issue as there will be a large enough sample for each year between all the counties.

3.1.2 New admissions with Diagnised Substance Abuse Problems

Looking at the scatterplot of the percent of admissions with a substance abuse problem it is not clear if men or women have a higher percentage of substance abuse problems, but looking at the means show that men have a higher avrage percentage of prison admissions with a substance abuse problem. The percentage of new admissions with a substance abuse problem seem to skew higher than those with opioid use, which makes sense as all those classified with opioid use are classified as having a substance abuse problem, but not all those with a substance abuse problem have used opioids. Additionally there appear to be two outliers in 2016 that have a percentage above 100%, which is not plausible.

This is confirmed by looking at the averages by gender and year as there are a higher percentage of men with opioid use than women. There also appears to be an outlier for women in 2016 with a percentage greater than 100%, which should not be possible.

4 Feature Engineering

4.1 Percent of Admissions with Diagnosed Substance Abuse Problem versus Scatterplot of Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use

With the exception of two outliers, most of the data appears to be in the upper triangular area of the graph. This can be interpreted as most observations having a higher percentage of inmates with a diagnose substance abuse problem than new admissions with opioid use. There appear to be a large number of observations at (0,0), (0,100), and (100,100), which could influence the regression model. For this analysis, I made the decision to remove observations where there were zero inmates screened as all of those observations would be at the point (0,0). Filtering them out will help with the density of observations at the point (0,0) and will give a more accurate analysis of the relationship between the percentage of inmate with a diagnosed substance abuse problem and the percentage of inmates with opioid use. For similar reason, I also filtered out instances where there was only one inmate screened as the percentage can only take on values of 0, or 100, which can also skew the endpoints to be heavier. By filtering out these instance I aim to make the data to look more normlly distributed as oppossed being a tail heavy distribution.

Additionally, I will filter out counties that are equal to “Commonwealth” as that is a summation of all the counties in Pennsylvania. Similarly, I will be removing observations where gender is equal to “All” because they are summations of male and female. The year variable will be recoded to be categorcial, with 2016 being the reference category as I am interested if there is difference in the relationship between years.

4.1.1 Percentage of Admissions with Diagnosd Substance Abuse Outliers

4.1.2 Percentage of New Admissions with Opioid Use Outliers

Filtering the data for the outliers shows that female admissions in Columbia county in 2016 is responsible for one of the outliers due to the same reason for the outlier with opioid use. The other outlier comes from quarter 1 of 2016 in Delaware county when 12 admissions were screened, but 15 had a substance abuse problem. The one for Columbia county should be corrected after correcting for the issue with opioid use percentage, and a similar approach will be used for Delaware county as well.

4.1.3 Percentage of New Admissions with Opioid Use Outliers

Filtering the data shows that the outlier again comes from Columbia county in quarter 1 of 2016 for women as they had 5 drug screened admissions, but 7 new admissions with opioid use. Furthermore, in quarter 1 of 2016 there were 4 new female admissions with opioid us, but there were no drug screened admissions. As the average TCU drug screen score is 5.5 for quarter 1 of 2016, it seems likely that there were new admissions screened.

Doing so would allow the percentage of inmates with a diagnosed substance abuse to be around 60%, and 80% for the percentage of new admissions with opiod use. This ensures that all values are plausible values for females in Columbia county.

5 Linear Regression

5.1 Baseline Linear Regression

## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = as.numeric(`Percent of Admissions with Diagnosed Substance Abuse Problem`) ~ 
##     `Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use` + `Year Category`, 
##     data = pa_educ_add_mod)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -73.026  -9.242   0.504  10.243  37.132 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                                             Estimate Std. Error t value
## (Intercept)                                 62.86837    0.92285  68.124
## `Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use`  0.26888    0.01252  21.479
## `Year Category`2017                          2.51443    1.11063   2.264
## `Year Category`2018                          6.77229    1.10468   6.131
## `Year Category`2019                          9.94596    1.10553   8.997
## `Year Category`2020                         10.15806    1.15097   8.826
## `Year Category`2021                          8.48070    1.14014   7.438
## `Year Category`2022                          5.38463    1.22513   4.395
##                                             Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)                                  < 2e-16 ***
## `Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use`  < 2e-16 ***
## `Year Category`2017                           0.0237 *  
## `Year Category`2018                         9.99e-10 ***
## `Year Category`2019                          < 2e-16 ***
## `Year Category`2020                          < 2e-16 ***
## `Year Category`2021                         1.35e-13 ***
## `Year Category`2022                         1.15e-05 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 16.28 on 2798 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.1759, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1739 
## F-statistic: 85.33 on 7 and 2798 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

For the first linear regression, I only include the variables related to the relationship I wish to analysize. For this model analyzing the relationship between the percentage of admissions with a substance abuse problem and the percentage of new admissions with opioid use controlling for year, all of the variables are significantly different from zero at the p=0.05 level. On average, a 1 percentage point increase in the percent of new admissions with opioid use leads to a 0.27 percentage point increase in the percent of admissions with a substance abuse problem. Looking at the residual plot of the model shows there to be no extreme outliers, but the Q-Q plot show the residuals to be tail heavy. Performing a Box-Cox transformation on the model shows the ideal transformation to be close to 2, so I will include a squared term of the explanatory variable in the model to see if that improves the residual plots.

5.1.1 Box-Cox Transformation

## Call:
## lm(formula = `Percent of Admissions with Diagnosed Substance Abuse Problem` ~

##         `Year Category`, data = pa_educ_add_mod)
##

##

## (Intercept)                                         6.422e+01  1.063e+00
## `Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use Squared` 9.792e-04  3.841e-04

## `Year Category`2017                                 2.477e+00  1.110e+00

## `Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use Squared`   2.550   0.0108 *  
## `Percent of New Admissions with Opioid Use`           4.981 6.71e-07 ***
## `Year Category`2017                                   2.232   0.0257 *  
## `Year Category`2018                                   6.136 9.68e-10 ***
## `Year Category`2019                                   8.986  < 2e-16 ***

## Multiple R-squared:  0.1778, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1755 
## F-statistic: 75.62 on 8 and 2797 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

Performing the Box-Cox transformation does not show much improvement in the Q-Q plot, likely due to the data being tail heavy on both sides of the distribution as discussed in earlier sections. The squared term does not appear to be significant at the p=0.05 level, so it would be best to leave it out of the model as it makes the model harder to interpret. Results may differ if the non-transformed explanatory variable was removed, but it is best practice to keep it in the model with higher order terms.

5.2 Full Model

This model includes all the variables as the baseline model, and also controls for county, gender, average TCU drug screen score, and number of drug screened admissions. There is also an interaction term between the percent of new admisssions with opioid use and year to control for if the percentage of new admissions with opioid use fluctuates between years.

Most of the variables in this model are significant at the p=0.05 level with the exception of the number of drug screened admissions and many of the counties. Additionally, the explanatory variable is also not significant, indicating that other variables in the model may be better predictors of the percent of admissions with a substance abuse problem. The residual plots for this model appear to have varying patterns that indicate they are not normally distributed. In the plot of the residuals versus the fitted values, there appear to be multiple diagnol lines as opposed to being randomly scattered. The right most prominent diagnol appears to be from counties that had a 100% of admissions with a substance abuse problem as the fitted value plus residual is equal to 100, so it is likely the other diagnols follow similar patterns for other values. There are no significant outliers in any of the plots that appear to have strong leverage over the model.

5.4 Model Comparisons

5.4.0.1 R-Squared of Baseline Model
## [1] 0.1759257

#####R-Squared of Model with Most Control Variable

## [1] 0.7485047
5.4.0.2 R-Square of Adjusted Model
## [1] 0.737607

Comparing the R-squared values of the models show the baseline model to have the lowest R-squared value and the full has the highest R-squared value. However, the adjusted model has a similar R-squared value as the model with the most control variables, so it terms of R-square it would be the best value.

5.4.0.3 Five-Fold Validation Between Baseline and Full Models

Completing a 5-fold cross validation between the first two models shows the model with more control variables (M2) to have a lower mean squared error than the baseline model (M1). The MSE is over three times larger on average for the baseline model, making it a worse predictor.

5.4.0.4 Five-Fold Validation Between Full and Adjusted Models

Comparing the MSE of the adjusted (M2) and full model (M1) shows them to have approximately the same average MSE for the 5-fold cross validation. The full model is slightly lower than the adjusted model, but the difference does appear to be large enough to include the extra variables in the full model.

5.5 Best Model

Overall, the baseline model performed the worst in terms of cross-validation and R-squared values. This model is best for observing the direct relationship between the percentage of admissions with a substance abuse problem and the percentage of new admissions with opioid use controlling for year. The full model with the most control variable in it performed the best for the R-square and cross-validation tests, but it comes at the cost of all the extra variables in it. The adjusted model performed nearly as well the full model with less variables, which is why it would be the best the model to use out of the three variables.

6 Logistic Models

To answer the question of if there is a relationship between if there is a high percentage of inmates with substance abuse and gender, a logistic model must be used. For this analysis a high percentage of inmates with substance abuse problem is considered to be 51% or higher to ensure a majority of the inmates have a substance abuse problem.

6.1 Baseline Logistic Model

The baseline logistic model measures the difference in the proportion of observations with high rates of admissions with a substance abuse problem between men and women. With p-value<0.05 we fail to reject the null hypothesis that there is no difference between men and women. On average, there is a 0.088 higher probability that observations of men only have high rates of admissions with a substance abuse problem. However, with an R-squared value of 0.02297, gender alone is not a good enough predictor.

The full logsitic model measures the same relationship as the baseline logistic model, but also includes controls for year, county, percent of new admissions with opioid use, average TCU drug screen score, number of drug screened admissions along with an interaction term between gender and year. The high correlation is likely due to the interaction term between year and gender.

To get the adjusted logistic model, I conducted a stepwise regression between the baseline logistic model and the full logistic model. This adjusted model measures the relation between a high percentage of admisssions with a substance abuse problem and gender while controlling for controls for year, county, percent of new admissions with opioid use, average TCU drug screen score, and number of drug screened admissions. With a similar R-square value to the full logistic model, and no severe correlation between variables, the adjusted logistic regression model appears to be better than the full logsitic model.

## [1] 0.9886396

Using a 5-fold cross validation of the AUC for the three models yiels an average AUC of 0.627 for the baseline model, 0.989 for the full logistic model, and 0.988 for the adjusted logistic model. Given how close the AUC value is for the full and ajusted logistic models, it makes senses to use the adjusted logisitic model as it has less variables in the model and is less complex. Overall, the adjusted logistic model is the best model given how close its values were to the final model despite not having the interaction term in the model.

7 Conclusion

For both the linear and logistic regressions the adjusted models performed the best out of the three models. While they did not outperform the full models, they were very close to the full models across all the tests while having less variables in the model. The baseline models are best for measuring the direct relationship we wish to observe, but may overestimate the relationship as they do not control for other factors that may influence the relationship.
